en: Homage to the Lord of the World.
[The text provided consists solely of two vertical bars (||), which in classical Indic scripts typically mark the end of a section or verse. [End of Section]
With devotion, I pay homage to the unsurpassed Guru, the Protector whose nature is the Dharmadhātu, who is the sole domain of Bodhisattvas, and who acts for the benefit of the world.
I possess no skill in the critical examination of textual commentaries;
this commentary has been written at the command of my guru, so you should forgive it.
Nevertheless, this is written for the sake of another who seeks it— not for my own memory, nor for anyone else like me who might be in need of it.

Here, this great scholar, the venerable Avadhūta Maitreyanātha—the supreme guru in the Kriyā, Caryā, Yoga, Yogottara, and Anuttarayoga Tantras—desiring to compose an exposition on initiation (*seka*) following the lineage of the Four Seals (*caturmudrā*) established by the noble Nāgārjunapāda, first extols the subject matter and pays homage to the syllable *Evaṃ*, which is the very nature of Wisdom and Means and constitutes the condensed meaning of the introductory statement of the scriptures: "We pay homage to the syllable *Evaṃ*, which is the cause of the four moments."
Wherein joys arise through differentiation for the sake of attaining enlightenment. || 1 ||
"Evam-kāram," and so forth:
we pay homage with body, speech, and mind—that is, we bow down—to the two syllables *e* and *vaṃ*, which consist of sound and take the form of the Dharma-mudrā.
For what purpose?
"For the sake of attaining enlightenment" means for the sake of reaching the state of a perfectly awakened Buddha; this is how it connects with what follows.
This syllable *evaṃ* is of great significance and great benefit.
As the Blessed One stated in the *Devendraparipṛcchā*: "The word 'evam' was uttered at the beginning by the All-Seeing One for a specific purpose."
Listen to that, O Lord of the Gods, exactly and in due order:
(1) Among the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma, the two syllables have been declared to be the father and mother, the support of all. (2)
The letter *e* is the mother, while the letter *va* is remembered as the father;
the *bindu* therein is their union, and that union is most wonderful.
(3) The letter *e* is said to be the lotus, and the letter *va* is indeed the vajra.
The *bindu* therein is the seed-syllable; from it, the three worlds are produced.
(4) The letter *e* is *prajñā*, while the letter *va* is the Lord of Rapture (*suratādhipa*).
The *bindu* is the *anāhata* principle, and all other syllables are born from it. (5)
He who, knowing reality, understands the two syllables of the Dharma-seal,
shall become a turner of the wheel of Dharma for all sentient beings. But that person who, without understanding them, constantly recites these two syllables—
He is outside the Buddha-dharmas, like a wealthy man deprived of his enjoyments. (7) Thus, the two-syllable *māyā* is established here as the Omniscient One;
for that purpose, it is recited at the beginning of the treatises on the True Dharma. (8)
Therefore, Śakra, Lord of the Gods, if you desire the eternal state, the True Dharma must be held in high esteem; remember this, lest you fall from the imperishable state.
(9) Thus it was said.
He qualifies the subject at hand by its being the cause of that [result]: "that which is the cause of the four moments.
It is that which is the cause—the efficient cause—of the four moments known as *vividha*, *vipāka*, *vimarda*, and *vilakṣaṇa*.
For the syllable *evaṃ* (evam) is the very nature of the *dharmamudrā*.
Furthermore, when the *dharmamudrā* is cultivated, it removes the afflictions along with their latent predispositions (*savāsanakleśa*).
And the differentiation of moments is based on the differentiation of that removal.
Therefore, the syllable *evaṃ* is the cause of the moments themselves.
Furthermore, it qualifies [the syllable] in the same manner: "wherein blisses arise by way of distinction.

This means that within that very reality—the knowledge of the path consisting of wisdom and method—blisses known as *ānanda*, *parama*, *virama*, and *sahaja* arise distinctly, unmixed, according to the differentiation of moments.

Therefore, the collective meaning is: we pay homage to that *evaṃkāra*, which is the cause of the four moments, and within which alone the blisses arise by way of distinction, for the sake of attaining enlightenment.
That which consists of resonance has been explained.
Now, the form of the syllable is explained.

We pay homage to the syllable *Evaṃ*, which is the very configuration of the written letter *E* according to the teacher’s instruction, and whose intrinsic nature is the *dharmodayā*. Alternatively, we pay homage to the syllable *Evaṃ*, which has this form because of the destruction of the *upasargas*, the casket of all Buddhas, the seal (*mudrā*) of the *dharmodayā*.
"The Dharmodaya has such a form," thus it was described by the Blessed One himself.
Thus:
"That which is divine in the shape of the letter E, adorned in its center with the syllable *vaṃ*,
is the abode of all blisses, a casket for the jewel of the Buddha."
Now, one might ask: "What is the purpose of this salutation? To this he says: "He who is the cause of the four moments.
This means he is the cause—the primary reason—for the four moments characterized by diverse ripening (*vipāka*), sublation (*vimarda*), and distinctness (*vilakṣaṇa*).
And the state of being a cause belongs even to the diverse [teachings], because they culminate in the grinding [of afflictions].
We shall explain this in detail in the section on the "Extensive Teaching" (*pravacanavistara*).
Furthermore, there is an act of homage toward the cause by way of resolute conviction in its fruit.
As it has been said: "The reality of the cause is exactly as the reality of the fruit is perceived.
Furthermore, he states another reason for the salutation: "Wherein blisses arise from the division [of the letters]."
The [four states] called Ānanda, Parama, Virama, and Sahaja arise therein without being mutually confused according to their distinctions.

Although the ablative case would have been expected by the rule *janikartuḥ prakṛtiḥ* ("the source of that which is born"), the use of the locative case in the word *yasmin* indicates that the intended meaning is "locus" (*ādhāra*).
Therefore, they arise therein and remain established therein.
For thus, from momentary knowledge,
bliss— which is indeed knowledge— is established in the syllable Evam.
The vow of all the Buddhas is established in Evaṃkāra:
Oṃ, Padma, support of bliss, giver of the bliss of great passion!
O you who partake in the four joys, O Viśva, hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ, perform my task!
Thus:
"And wherever on the earth the Tathāgatas have stood, walked, or sat,
and wherever lion-thrones were prepared for them— to those places I bow."
This is because of the teaching.
For what purpose do we pay homage?
It is for the sake of attaining enlightenment—that is to say, for the sake of attaining the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are, which is to say, for the sake of perfect buddhahood.
The phrase "the cause of the four moments" refers to the reason for the salutation.
In that regard, what are those four moments,
and what is their sequence?
Therefore he says: "From that, the maturation (vipāka) is variegated; but in the third, it is of a different character.
And from that, the 'crushing' (vimarda) is to be known, due to the rejection of forceful yoga (haṭhayoga). (2)
"Variegated," and so forth.
Now, one might ask: why is something distinct from the sequence taught in the Tantras desired at this third [stage]?
To address that, he says: "Because of the rejection of Haṭhayoga."
In this regard, this is *haṭhayoga*: *vicitra* (the variegated) consists of various states such as embracing, arising from the duality of the grasped and the grasper;
*vipāka* (ripening) is its opposite, being non-variegated due to the absence of the grasped, consisting of the blissful enjoyment of knowledge during friction (*ghṛṣṭi*);
and *vimarda* (crushing) is non-conceptual vision, the blissful jewel, extending up to the pinnacle of pervasion (*vyāpyagra*).
One state is distinct and devoid of passion (*rāga*) because of the absence of intense bliss;
the other is not devoid of passion because, through the recollection of the experience of bliss, there is no absence of detachment (*virāga*) at the time of falling [from the peak].
As it has been said: "The manifold is known as diverse, consisting of embracing, kissing, and so forth."
The ripening is its opposite; happiness is the enjoyment of knowledge.
Vimarda is said to be reflection, such as thinking, "I have enjoyed happiness";
vilakṣaṇa is other than these three, being free from both attachment and detachment.

Thus, according to the view of the proponents of formlessness (nirākāravādin), this experience of the jewel— which resembles the cloudless midday sky in autumn, being level and consisting of pure consciousness alone— remains free from the stain of the entire circle of forms such as blue and so forth.
However, the proofs refuting these forms, such as the argument from the exclusion of being one or many, are not elaborated here for fear of prolixity.
As they say: "Therefore, that which appears as gross does not exist in objects nor in cognition, because it has been refuted in one case; it is likewise impossible even in many cases."
This other internal division appears as if it were external;
for the appearance of differentiation within non-differentiated cognition is indeed a cognitive distortion.
Thus, this very [state] is the dharmakāya;
following that, the gnosis appearing in the form of the maṇḍala circle and so forth is the sambhogakāya.
The emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) consists of the elements and elemental derivatives, appearing in forms such as Śākyamuni and others.
The fact that these possess a single intrinsic nature is the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*). Likewise, the Dharma is the state of being thoroughly refined.
The maturation is the enjoyment body;
the manifold is the emanation body;
and that which is devoid of characteristics is the essential body.
As it has been said: "The latter two are the form-bodies (*rūpakāya*).

Because of the statement, "One should meditate until [the object] becomes non-apprehendable," this very thing—characterized by the example—is that which will bring about the accomplishment of the forms of the maṇḍala circle and so forth when meditated upon through diligent, uninterrupted, and long-term practice; namely, the enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the emanation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), by the power of previous vows.
Alternatively, this bliss that has been experienced will itself attain clarity through meditation characterized by diligence and the like.

As they say: "Therefore, whether it be real or unreal, whatever is intensely meditated upon, when the power of that meditation is perfected, its fruit is a cognition that is vivid and non-conceptual. Here too, by the force of the impetus of previous vows, the two form bodies [arise].

And this indeed is the means of entry, as it has been said: "By means of the mandala-circle and so forth, and by the sequence of self-consecration. And for this very reason, this alone is proclaimed as the meaning of the Middle Way.
"Because of the non-interruption of self-awareness, because of the non-existence of blue and so forth,
and because of the non-arising of causal signs, the Middle Way is held.
Here, the "non-arising of causal signs" is intended to mean the absence of dogmatic adherence (*abhiniveśa*).
Because of the absence of attachment to existence, non-existence, and so forth, there is the state of being devoid of the four extremes;
furthermore, the "fourth" [state] is also present here, according to the statement, "That fourth is likewise.

This refers to the formless cognition experienced in the *prajñājñāna*; the word "likewise" (*tathā*) means that when the impurity of the circle of forms such as blue has been removed, it should be understood as being like the *prajñājñāna*.
The proponents of the theory of mental images (*sākāravādin*), however, maintain that cognition devoid of an image is not experienced even in dreams;
as they say: "There is no functioning of the intellect apart from the wheel of images; when that [view] is refuted, the glory of victory belongs to the powerful Middle Way (*madhyamaka*).

If this faultless, manifold, and non-dual mind is not accepted, then what room is there for one who maintains the absence of images?"* Thus it is said. *This verse is cited from Śāntarakṣita’s *Madhyamakālaṃkāra*, verse 9.*
And one should not think that because there is no manifestation of a form (*ākāra*), the form does not exist prior [to cognition];

for even in the absence of a definitive determination (*niścaya*) of it, there exists the experience of the cognition of blue and so forth—which cannot be denied—and which is determined by a subsequent reflective awareness (*pṛṣṭhollekha*).
As they say: "In whatever manner a cognition appears, it is experienced exactly in that way; thus, there would indeed be a single nature for the variegated form within the mind."
Therefore, the realization of manifold non-duality alone is supreme;
and here too, for fear of excessive prolixity, no investigation into proving or refuting arguments has been undertaken.
They also reconcile this very point with the meaning of the Middle Way by virtue of its being devoid of the four logical extremes.

And so it has been said: "If the world is not non-existent, because its nature is luminosity; nor existent, because it is other than that [luminosity]; nor both, because it is one; nor neither, because it is not those two—then, being thus free from the four peaks [of conceptual extremes], what is the distinction between the Bhāṣyakāra’s view and the Madhyamaka?
Thus, by means of the difference created through exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), the *vimarda* state is a quality (*dharma*) that is non-different from the *sambhoga*.
The maturation body, the enjoyment body,
the manifold emanation body, and the characteristic-free essential body.

Wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), which is the defining characteristic, when practiced in that very manner, becomes further expressible by the term "the fourth," and being endowed with seven limbs, it would be the goal to be accomplished; therein,
the seven limbs consist of the enjoyment of wealth.

The "union" (*saṃpuṭa*) is the great bliss (*mahāsukha*) arising from meditative attainment; it is devoid of intrinsic nature because it is free from conceptual construction, due to its being of the nature of pleasure.
It is "filled with compassion" because it performs the welfare of sentient beings through the enjoyment body (*sambhogakāya*) and so forth, by the force of the impetus of previous vows;
it is "uninterrupted" because there is no interval in between;
and it is "unceasing" because its flow is not cut off.

As it has been said: "In this world, my desired goal is that which is endowed with these seven very limbs—enjoyment, union, great bliss, the absence of intrinsic nature, compassion, fullness, and uninterrupted non-ceasing—and is praised by those whose intellects have been refined by valid cognition.
Or rather, enough with this practice involving the yoga of the seven limbs.
There is indeed no fixed rule here,
since the circle of yoginīs, when meditated upon as being devoid of self (nairātmya), is the cause of Buddhahood;
nevertheless, in this case, our means of accomplishment consists of the yoga of the seven limbs.

Because of the absence of a [separate] *saṃpuṭa*, it has been said: "If that very thing which is to be accomplished—endowed with its seven limbs—is itself the means of accomplishment, why is the wheel of the Yoginīs of Nairātmyā not accepted for the sake of awakening? Thus.

Now, if this is the thought—that even there, the state of being encapsulated by the *khaṭvāṅga* as a means exists—then consider what was said: "The goddess Nairātmyā-Yoginī, endowed with the enjoyment [of the senses] and other qualities, is encapsulated by the *khaṭvāṅga*; alas, what practice (*sādhana*) is not for awakening? Thus it is.
That too is not tenable;

for even in the Pāramitā-naya, although there is no intended [literal] union (*saṃpuṭa*), because the union of the bodhicitta consisting of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*) occurs, it would follow that the accomplishment of the goal endowed with the seven limbs—just as in the Mantra-naya—would be attained. This is so unless one abandons the specific [literal] union and conceives of it otherwise.

Because of the union of emptiness and its opposite, there would be a logical fallacy in another system. Now, if it is argued that in this practice (*sādhana*) there is indeed the possession of the seven limbs—since "having taken the two breasts, the *bola* (male organ) becomes situated in the middle of the *kakkola* (female organ); the two banks become the bell (*ghaṇṭā*), and the stamen becomes the *bolaka*"—that too is not well-founded, because all of this pertains to the state of accomplishment (*siddhi-avasthā*) and not to the state of practice (*sādhana-avasthā*).

Therefore, even in the absence of such a means, the consequence that the accomplishment of the goal endowed with its seven limbs would follow is difficult to avoid even in the Pāramitā system. [One might argue: "First, the state of being unsealed (asampuṭatā) is to be cultivated; once [the deity] is perfected, that [seal] will occur. This is our accepted proof, and not otherwise. Thus.
And others describe this very state as "non-duality like an illusion" (*māyopamādvaita*);

for example, the experience of sexual pleasure with a beloved woman experienced in a dream is not false because it is subsequently experienced by another dream-consciousness that follows it— since its experience is not absolutely annihilated— nor is it non-deceptive in the same way as objects perceived during the waking state that perform causal functions and are cognized by oneself and others.

Regarding this, they say: "When one dream arises from another dream, then the variety of consciousness is indeed unreal; yet it is not real because of the awareness of its unreality, nor is there annihilation because of its manifestation.
Thus, in the same way, this entire universe is not unreal through absolute annihilation, because it is experienced.

Nor is it ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), because—as stated in the passage beginning with "because the arising of the existent and the non-existent is impossible"—it is impossible for that which is determined to be dependently originated to exist as something ultimately unarisen, since it has not arisen at all from the perspective of ultimate reality.
As it has been said: "That which is dependently originated is not arisen by way of its own-being (*svabhāva*);

how can that which is not arisen by way of its own-being be called 'arisen'? Furthermore, in this case as well, the establishment of its possession of the fourfold nature, the *dharmakāya*, and so forth, should be understood in the same manner as before.

Now, one might object: "Is not *haṭhaseka* (forceful sprinkling) applied by compulsion? That is to say, it is irrational. If one asks how it is irrational, it is said: because it contradicts the scriptures (*āgama*).

To demonstrate that, he says: "If [the first stage] is observation (*ālocana*) and [the second] is crushing (*vimarda*), how can a third be intended? For in that case, there would be no observation at all, as consciousness would lack its defining characteristic. Regarding the phrase "observation" and so forth:
between the supreme (*para*) and the cessation (*virama*), one should observe the object and make it firm; here, the "middle" (*madhya*) between these two is what is intended.
And that [property] does not exist in your view,
because this [statement] has a different purpose.
For this genitive case is used in the sense of selection;
therefore, the meaning is that between two, whichever is superior is to be taken here.

And since the "best" is indeed the *virama* [joy], nothing is inconsistent here; however, the statement— "The beginning of *virama* is beyond the supreme (*parama*), and from the void (*śūnya*) comes the Heruka of the void"— is not tenable, for in this context, the beginning of *virama* is intended to be beyond the supreme.
That too is not so,
because here the meaning is entirely different:
it is "viramādi," where *virama* is that which begins (*ādi*).
And its status as "the first" (*āditva*) is relative to the co-emergent (*sahaja*);
therefore, this point is also well-established.
If that is so, how can it be said: "Then one should characterize [the state] at the beginning of the *virāma*, and that is devoid of the three joys"? ♭ Thus [it is asked].
In this case as well, it should be understood as before that "this is the cessation (*virama*) and it is the beginning (*ādiśva*).
If so, how is it that [the text] says, "The *vimarda* is declared to be reflection (*ālocana*), and 'happiness has been enjoyed by me'?"

For here, the conceptual nature of the words *vimarda* and so forth is clearly understood; if, on the other hand, there were somehow a designation of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatva*) in this context, even that would be refuted by the contradiction with worldly convention. To illustrate: people understand *vimarda* as dispute, *kṣodana* as investigation, and *ālocana* as reflection upon various effects and so forth.

Furthermore, in the *vicitra* [state] there is the first bliss (*prathamānanda*), in the *vipāka* the supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), in the *vimarda* the cessation-bliss (*viramānanda*), and in the *vilakṣaṇa* the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). Regarding this, it is certain that *vimarda* is indeed *virama*. Moreover, the first bliss has the form of the world (*jagadrūpa*), and the supreme bliss is likewise the world.
The innate (sahaja) does not exist within the three [joys], including the joy of cessation (viramānanda) and the world itself.
Thus, by describing the *virama* as having the nature of the world (*jagad-rūpa*), its state of being *saṃsāra* has been declared.

And in this way, because of the statement that "saṃsāra is mere conceptual construction" (*vikalpa-mātra*), its state of possessing conceptual construction (*savikalpatva*) would be asserted; yet, since its state of being free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpatva*) is intended through its innate nature (*sahajatā*), even this [previous position] falls apart.
And thus, even this [notion] that "I am of the nature of innate bliss (sahajānanda), which is the supreme limit beginning with the stage of cessation (virama)" falls apart; likewise,
the great bliss called "innate" (sahaja) is that which is to be accomplished in the Yoginītantra.
"Furthermore, the vision occurs at the end of the supreme [joy] and with effort at the beginning of the cessation [joy]"—such statements as these would also be contradicted;
likewise: "First is the vase consecration, second is the supreme secret, third is the knowledge of wisdom, and fourth is that again in the same way."

As for the consecration of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*), it is the consecration of the co-emergent (*sahajābhiṣeka*), because even this [wisdom] is not obstructed. Therefore, by resolving such passages [as those cited], since there would be a contradiction with the scriptures, one must not maintain that in the third [empowerment] there is a crushing (*vimarda*) consisting of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); for therein exists only non-conceptual experience (*nirvikalpakavedana*). He concludes that very point with its elaboration: "Therefore, it is logical to understand the third [empowerment] as having a distinct characteristic."

Through self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), there is accomplishment, and the meaning of the scripture (*āgama*) is also consistent. The passage beginning with "it is of a different character" (*vilakṣaṇam*) and so forth is easy to understand. Now, one might object: since the contradiction of worldly consensus (*lokaprasiddhi*) does not constitute a valid sublation (*bādhaka*), how can sublation be shown by the passage beginning with "perception (*ālocana*) and deliberation (*vimarda*)"?
This [objection] is likewise merely the result of your failure to understand our intended meaning.

Since the statement "the world itself is the joy of cessation" contradicts the premise that the world is the nature of *vimarda* (the stage of friction), it subverts all the aforementioned scriptures; consequently, even the passage beginning with "perception" (*ālocana*) is likewise subverted. Therefore, the contradiction is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "perception. For this very reason, the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna also, in the *Caturmudrānvaya*, demonstrated the contradiction by stating: "Having observed the object between the supreme joy (*paramānanda*) and the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*), make it firm. If that is so, then in your own system, there must be some pleasure through *ānanda*, and *paramānanda* must be superior to that.
"Detachment arises from the joys of cessation (*viramānanda*); that innate joy (*sahajānanda*), however, is what remains. How is this to be understood?
It should be known thus:

because the joys (*ānanda*) and the supreme cessations (*paramavirama*) are used to denote slight pleasure and the detachment exceeding it, "what remains" (*śeṣataḥ*)—by way of elimination (*pāriśeṣyataḥ*) as something other than those three—is to be understood as the innate joy (*sahajānanda*).

Alternatively, although it was stated thus according to the sequence "bliss, supreme, cessation, and the innate" (*ānanda-parama-virama-sahaja*), it should be understood that the *sahaja* is indeed the third;
if this is so, why was the *suṣeka* (the excellent emission) alone not shown by the Blessed One?
Why has this sequence— consisting of *ānanda*, *parama*, *virama*, and *sahaja*— been shown as a source of doubt involving strenuous and forced cultivation?
It is because the demonstration of this sequence depends entirely upon a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who dispels the intellectualism derived from books.
As it has been said: "Enlightenment indeed depends upon spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*), and likewise elsewhere: "It is obtained when the Guru is pleased.

Therefore, by refuting forced initiation (*haṭhaseka*) and difficult initiation (*duḥseka*) through this lack of contradiction, the systematic arrangement of the formless (*nirākāra*) and so forth is certainly not refuted.

Because that [practice] is contradictory up to the distance of one *yojana*, this entire systematic arrangement should be understood as established solely by the doctrine of the excellent consecration (*suṣeka*) in the form of the Vajradhara’s consolation.

Even those who advocate for the difficult consecration (*duḥseka*) through forceful means describe it in this way; therefore, it has been shown here for that purpose. Immediately following this, he describes the difficult consecration: "The variegated [consecration] occurs during kissing and embracing; that named 'ripening' (*vipāka*) occurs during friction."

Those for whom [the emission] is distinct from the jewel (maṇi) possess the realization of a "difficult consecration" (duḥseka). Beginning with the act of kissing and so forth, up until the friction (ghṛṣṭi)—that is, the external action starting from the union of the *bola* and *kakkola* until the arrival at the moon-jewel (*maṇi*)—therein lies the maturation (*vipāka*). Having obstructed the jewel, up until the place to be described, it is "distinct. Those who maintain this view are said to have the realization of a difficult consecration.

With the word "saṃ" (well), he derides them. To refute them, he says: "If that cognition which occurs in the *Ratnagarbha* were itself the reality (*tattva*), then it would be the Śaiva Veda; for this is not accepted by the Buddhists. [The word] "ratna" and so forth refers to what belongs to Śiva as "Śaiva."

"This is the Veda of the Veda. Now, one might ask: "Does this apply to the Śaiva scriptures and others as well? To this he says: "And likewise, in the *Devīparipṛcchā* and the *Śivanirnāda-tantra*, [it is said]: 'O Goddess, this City of Jewels (*ratnapura*) becomes water in the pericarp;
Rudra is in the pair, Śiva is the most excellent, and she herself is the Power (*śakti*) higher than the highest. Thus begins the passage starting with 'the City of Jewels'."
A *ratna* is a jewel; that very thing is the city (*pura*), the abode, of that which is desired as the nature of bliss— that is the "jewel-city" (*ratnapura*)—
fallen upon the filaments (*kiñjalka*).
The Lord Rudra [perceives] the insubstantiality of the burning within the union of the two in meditative absorption.
Śiva is the bringer of auspiciousness,
and for that very reason he is supreme;
he alone is the reality, and his power (śakti) is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpā).

"Higher than the highest," "the highest," that very same [state]. He describes its essential nature: "Free from both the object of definition and the definition itself, devoid of verbal expression, a wondrous bliss arises from the union of Śiva and Śakti. The passage beginning with "object of definition" is easy to understand. Showing that this very [state] is the supreme universal form (viśvarūpa), he says: "In reality, entities do not exist as they appear, being merely conceived through the form of power (śakti)."

Power, however, is the vision of emptiness, which destroys all superimpositions. [The statement] "external entities such as form and so forth do not exist" means that they do not exist in reality—that is, from the perspective of ultimate truth. If that is so, how then does the appearance of blue and other such objects occur?
Therefore he says: "cultivated in the form of power" means that the conscious selves have attained the nature of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).
If that were so, then that [power] alone would be the ultimately real (*paramārthasatī*).
Therefore, he says "power" (*śakti*) and so forth for the purpose of refuting that [position];
this is easily understood and is itself devoid of the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
This has been stated in the *Bhargaśikhā*, a Śākta Tantra: "It is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor is it devoid of both;

for that state is difficult to discern—it is some ineffable, unsurpassed reality. He expresses the same point in another way in the *Ucchuṣmatantra* as well: "From the union of Śiva and Śakti, there arises the supreme non-duality, which is the void (*kha*) among existing things.
It is neither Śiva nor Śakti, abiding like [a gem] within a jewel. [The passage begins with: "Śiva... and so forth.

"Situated within the jewel" means residing in the center of the *maṇi*. Regarding the steadfastness of the yogin who has realized this knowledge, [the Lord] says in the Yoga-chapter: "For the yogin who is satisfied by the nectar of knowledge and has accomplished all that was to be done, there remains nothing whatsoever to be done; if there were anything to be done, he would not be a knower of reality. (Yoga Sūtra 3.50). The passage beginning with "by the nectar of knowledge" is easy to understand. Now, a proponent of Vedānta might perhaps offer this description regarding that which has come down through the sequence of the traditional scriptures (*āmnāya*) about to be stated:

Therefore, for the sake of understanding that [knowledge], and not for the sake of abandoning it, he states the first half [of the verse]: "Even for the Vedāntins, knowledge is beyond the senses and is consciousness (*avitti*); according to Bhāskara, it is consciousness, while according to the followers of the Lord (*bhagavad-vādin*), it is pure bliss (*ānanda-mātra*) alone. (12) Regarding the phrase "beyond the senses" and so forth:
"They say the senses are superior; superior to the senses is the mind."
"But the intellect is higher than the mind, and that which is higher than the intellect is He.

This having been said, the remainder is easily understood. Even in the Vedānta of the Lord’s established doctrine, he states what was previously mentioned as characterized by the illustration: "From the agitation caused by the union with Śakti, the bliss that culminates in the immersion into Śakti—that bliss of the reality of Brahman is called one's own innate bliss. (13) "Śakti," and so forth.
"Power" (śakti) refers to Lalanā; "union with her" means contact, and from that contact comes agitation, and from that, movement.

Regarding the phrase "concluding with the immersion into power" (*śaktyāveśāvasānikam*): "power" (*śakti*) refers to the woman; "immersion" (*āveśa*) is the intense absorption or ever-increasing passion for her. "Concluding with that" (*tadavasānikam*) means the bliss arising at its limit. That bliss of the reality of Brahman—that is, the reality of gnosis—is called "one's own" (*svākyam*), meaning it is one's very own. By this, he declares the similarity [of this bliss] to that which resides within the *kapāla* (cranial vessel) located between the *bola* (linga) and its tip, at the moment when the joy of sexual union has emerged from all women.
"Until another consciousness arises, there is no emergence of the Kaula scripture"—from such a statement [it follows]. To demonstrate the nature of this [consciousness], he says:
"There is no arrival of sufferings; therein is uninterrupted bliss.
Bliss is the form of Brahman, and that is manifested in liberation. (14)
The passage beginning with "of sufferings" and so forth is easy to understand.
By this very [verse], he declares the world to be of the nature of Brahman: "Whatever is seen, one should conceive that as Brahman;
then the mind, no longer directed toward anything else, abides in Brahman alone. (15)
The passage beginning with "yadyat" and so forth is easy to understand.

Immediately following this, he speaks in praise of the woman who is the cause of this knowledge: "What can be attained by other visions that cannot be attained by the sight of one's beloved alone—that through which even a mind still possessed of passion reaches nirvāṇa? (16)
Regarding "priyā" and so forth:
liberation is seen as dear because it is perceived by her; having established that it is indeed dear, the remainder is easy to understand.
By this, it is stated that even for them, having set aside other interpretations, only the *lalana* is intended for the purpose of illustrating the example.

Now, for one who has thus entered [the path], he teaches the abandonment of all attachment: "Abandon dharma and adharma; abandon both truth and falsehood. Having abandoned both truth and falsehood, abandon that by which you abandon. (17)
"Abandon," and so forth, is easy to understand.
And it is said that [reality] is devoid of the four logical alternatives; even in the Bhagavadgītā: "The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being;
for the end of both of these has been seen by the seers of truth. (2.16)
The passage beginning with "nāsataḥ" and so forth is easy to understand.

Having stated the similarity with other scriptures, he now states the contradiction with his own scripture: "Furthermore, if the unshakeable mind (*akṣobhya-citta*) is said to be empty of the apprehended object and so forth, there is a contradiction with our own scripture due to the separation from the *vajrasattva-mudrā*. (19)
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "And what [more]":
here, indeed, the meaning investigated in the Madhyamaka and other systems is elucidated in the Mantra system by means of the fruit, which is the yoga with the deity (*devatāyoga*).

Therefore, on the principle that "whatever is sealed by something becomes of the same nature as that," the four [Buddhas] such as Vairocana—who are of a dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*)—are described as the subjects (*grāhaka*) for the sake of abandoning the objectivity (*grāhyatva*) of the objects of perception, namely the four aggregates (*skandha*) of form and so forth, which possess a nature of being perceived.

Furthermore, if it is asserted that for the sake of their seals (*mudrā*), Akṣobhya—who is of a perfected nature and empty of subject and object—is [the deity], then this contradicts the Vajrasattva-seal mentioned in the scriptures;
for within the bodhicitta residing in Ratnagarbha and others, there exists an Akṣobhya of an unperfected nature.
And since the Buddhist tenet does not arise without the Vajrasattva-seal, how is it that there is no similarity with the external [non-Buddhist] systems?

And likewise, if there were not this single teaching of emptiness here, then for one who makes the distinction between the Buddhist and the outsider— when everything, including Kambalāmbarapāda, is analyzed with an intellect sharpened by subtle scrutiny— the final conclusion would be the same for all. (3)
For this very reason, out of fear that consciousness might become established [as a real entity], the Sage—
having spoken and then spoken again of the Dharma of the teaching by means of its nature as emptiness— distinguishes [the latter from the former]. Thus,
even the entire *pravacana* (scriptural teaching) was composed by Īśvara and others, who have mastered all the Vedas.
"The distinction of the Buddhist tantras and mantras regarding emptiness [is as follows].

Thus, since the distinction between the Tathāgata’s teachings on emptiness and the assertions of emptiness imagined by others is clearly established by way of their underlying intention (*abhisandhi*), it need not be elaborated further.
If this is so, for what purpose then is this taught?
To this he says: "For what purpose is this taught by the teachers of this system as a rule?
It is first revealed with the intention of providing consolation to the Tathāgatas. (20)
"For what purpose," and so forth:
"the consolation of the Tathāgata" means the consolation provided by the Tathāgata;
and the Tathāgata is Vairocana.
Since it serves as an illustration, by the mention of Ratnasambhava and the others, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi are included;
their "reassuring" consists in their being made conscious through being sealed by Akṣobhya.
"By that mind" means by that cognition.

Now, he shows in which place each respective proponent exists: "In the *bolagarbha*, some describe it as having form (*sākāra*) and others as being formless (*nirākāra*); some describe it as the Middle Way (*madhyamā*), but 'not so,' according to our Guru’s vision. (21)
The seed-syllable and so forth are with form within the womb, while that which is before it is formless;
or else, that which is before it is with form, while that within its womb is formless.
And likewise, that description which is middling is not the view of our teachers.
Why?
He says: "Whether it has fallen upon the Vajragarbha, at its tip, or into the skull-cup, the reality is not desired even in the intermediate space; it is known from the mouth of the Guru. (22)
Since [the position] beginning with "vajra" is not desired,
why is there even this non-desire?

Vajragarbha replied: "In that regard, because of the non-separation from the Vajrasattva-mudrā due to the existence of Akṣobhya in the form of pleasure (*sāta*) at its peak, [this applies] both in the intermediate space and in the skull-cup (*kapāla*). Let alone the non-separation from the Vajrasattva-mudrā—because of the state of experiencing determined pleasure, there is also separation from the Akṣobhya-mudrā by way of the nature of the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and so forth.
And this is obtained through the application of the previously mentioned phrase, 'due to the non-separation from the Vajrasattva-mudrā.'"
If so, where is reality (tattva) to be known?
"Reality is known from the mouth of the Guru through wealth [of realization]"—
by this it is traditionally taught that reality is where the Blessed One, who holds the sixteen, the half, and the quarter-bindu, resides.
Regarding this, they say: "Both cheeks are equal, both are swollen; the arrow falls, while I remain here."
Falling like arrows, unshakable, closing their eyes and winking,
with the arrow as the object and the cause sealed— this is that kingdom of great bliss.

In these two—the Vajra-form and the Sattva-form—Vajrasattva is emptiness and compassion, wisdom and means, and nirvāṇa and saṃsāra. This very meaning is shown by the Blessed One in various places in the *utpattikrama* as the two drops (*bindu*) situated above and below in the center of the moon and sun during the melting [of passion] through great desire (*mahārāga*). As for the *niṣpannakrama*, it is the aforementioned meaning of consecration (*sekārtha*).

The perfected [nature], however, arises from the fluid as the Lord, whose form is the sun and the *bola*, consisting of wisdom and means, having the nature of emptiness and compassion, and whose essence is the *dharmadhātu*; his standing on a single big toe indicates that he has not been affected by the state of faltering.
But if this is so— [it has been said] "one should again visualize the reality-syllable *hūṃ* situated in the center of the vajra-navel"— how is it that [the objection] does not hold here,
since the meaning of "situated in the center of the vajra-navel" is contradicted?
Because this has another meaning:

for it is intended that one should meditate on the reality of *hūṃ* as situated between the two excellent limbs of wisdom and method—the *vajra* and the *varaṭaka*—as being "ha" (empty of cause), "ū" (free from conceptual construction), and "aṃ" (non-abiding).
If that is so, how can it be said to be "within the jewel"?
It is said:
even here, there is a different meaning;
for thus, it is well established that [the essence] is contained within the two jewels, the lotus and the thunderbolt.
Now, how is it understood that this is the intended meaning in both cases?

It is said: "In the sky of the lotus, at the point of pressure between the jewel and the pericarp, one should gaze at the mind within the jewel from the *vajraparyaṅka* posture; whatever gnosis arises, that gnosis is of that very nature. Thus, according to the *Paramādya-tantra*.
The meaning here is as follows:

"in the lotus" (*kamale*) means in the space of the center of the lotus; "at the place of pressure," that is, at the point of contact between the "excellent jewel" (*maṇivaraṭaka*) and the "lotus-thunderbolt" (*paṅkajakuliśa*), [is expressed by] *vajraparyaṅkataḥ*. This means from the thunderbolt (*vajra*) on all sides (*pari*) and from its embrace (*aṅkataḥ*). By the use of the ablative case, it is intended to mean merely being attached externally to the thunderbolt.
The meaning is that the nature of consciousness is that cognition which arises for one who gazes at the *ī* situated within the two jewels (*maṇi*).

And so it is said in the *Vajrāmṛta*: "O Goddess, situated in the center of the navel, in the hidden sphere of the pericarp, it flows in the form of semen, residing between the vulva and the phallus."
And it is said in the *Hevajra*: "The seed-syllable of Kālī, [formed by] the moon and the sun, should be situated in the center.
Likewise:

"As long as the cool-rayed liquid of the stream of nectar, consisting of luminosity, does not fall into the interior of the petals of the Goddess’s lotus, having become of one flavor with the hosts of Jinas..."

Know that the innate form of the Lord, the cause of the world, is that which is pierced by compassion at the tip of the flashing vajra-peak; it is the innate nature of the glorious Karuṇābala as long as the moon, falling through the fire of the three vajras, remains within the hollow of the lotus-cup by the force of the wind, while its desire is dissolved in this momentary, well-hollowed cottage. That very mind which has arisen at this moment—devoid of the conceptualization of self and other, and free from activity—is indeed the innate; this we know clearly once more through reasoning and scripture.

When the supreme bliss of the union of wisdom and the lotus-vajra remains as the sole remainder, the drop (bindu) purified by the flow from its station becomes immovable; as long as the moon [of the bindu] is thus considered, the mind is unshakable and the moving stream of the winds is destroyed. Then the ear does not hear and the eye does not move—this is sought as Mahāmudrā.
It is not described by another, for the Innate (sahaja) is not found in anything else.
It has been stated: "One knows [the truth] for oneself through merit and by attending upon the guru during the sacred festivals (parvan).
How is it that, in this context, the "guru-parvan" refers to the "vajra-parvan"?
Since there is no semantic connection for the term "time of service" (*sevākāla*) and because there is an absence of attendance,
it is not said that "service is near the vajra" by means of the prefix *upa* denoting proximity.
In that case, regarding the statement "the bliss of *bola* is Mahāmudrā, the Vajra-āyatana is the Upāya," how is it that here too the bliss of *bola* is Mahāmudrā?
Because it is not connected to any external object, the meaning is that the vajra itself is the sense-field (*āyatana*), the locus, and the means;
and that which resides in the vajra-sense-field— the bliss of the *bola* and the *mahāmudrā*— is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).
It has been shown that this is a means (*upāya*); moreover, in our own system,
[the statement] "Now, therefore, I shall speak of the secret (*rahasya*) in brief and not in detail," as well as "in the supreme secret" (*parame rahasye*), and so forth, is well-established.
For the connection is as follows: "In the secret [place], I shall speak the secret.
Regarding "secret" (*rahasye*): *raha* refers to the vajra and the lotus; [the secret] is that which is between those two in every respect.
Yeti, having reached suchness as it truly is, is non-dual,
free from affliction, and transcends all limits.

And so it has been said: "The letter *ra* is declared to be the *vajra*, and the letter *ha* is called the *padma*. Now, for the sake of establishing the manifold (*vicitra*) [joy], he says: "Manifold is known as diverse," and so forth. How is it well-established? "Situated within the jewel," and so forth; it is perfectly conjoined with the Guru.

"Variegated" (*vicitra*) and so forth, [is explained] by the passage beginning with "of the guru" and so on [... because of the enumeration: "variegated" means manifold, such as embracing, kissing, and so forth.
For here, by the inclusion of the word "beginning" (ādi), everything from that point up to the stage of *ghṛṣṭi* is intended to be manifold;
indeed, how is it understood that it extends up to *ghṛṣṭi*, [as in the verse]: "And having embraced with both arms a sixteen-year-old woman who is wisdom itself"?

Based on the instruction, "The sprinkling by the Ācārya is considered to result from the union of the bell and the vajra," the "union of the bell and the vajra" here is intended to mean the touching of the lotus and the vajra.
Now, one might ask: how is it to be known that this is the master-initiation (*ācāryaseka*), and that the master is "variegated" (*vicitra*) at the beginning?
[The answer is: Ānanda and the others are to be known sequentially by the number of four sprinklings.
From this specific indication,

it should be understood according to their respective order that here there are four— namely, Ānanda and the others— as well as the four consisting of the Master (ācārya), the Secret (guhya), Wisdom (prajñā), and the Fourth (caturtha-tatpunaḥ).

And bliss (*ānanda*) is indeed manifold at every moment; thus, up to the point of friction, there is a manifold ripening (*vipāka*). Because that bliss is the enjoyment of knowledge—which is the reversal of that [ordinary] perversion—it is designated as such. Up to the tip of the jewel (*maṇyagra*), it is "supreme" because it consists of supreme bliss.
But how is it that,
when supreme bliss— which is devoid of multiplicity— has been attained in this moment, the Teacher would say, "O Mahāsattva, this great happiness is to be maintained"?
Because of the indication by the syllable *b*,
everything is well-established, since the meaning of "in this very moment," and so forth, exists precisely here where diversity is excluded;
and the passage beginning with "contained within the jewel" has already been explained.

If bliss up to the stage of *ghṛṣṭi* is the *ācārya*, and that which is before the *maṇi* is the supreme (*parama*), and that which is secret (*guhya*) is likewise [the *guhya*], then how is it that through the purification by laughter one is the *ācārya*, through vision the *guhyaka*, and furthermore, through the attainment of the hands in the *dvandva-yoga*, [one is the *prajñā*]?
If it is to be understood through external generation,
then how is that which is called the teacherhood of the water-initiation and so forth to be known?
That too must be known through external generation.

In the *Tathāgatāśvāsānanda*, the state of being an ācārya is established through the profound arising; and in the *Vajradharāśvāsānanda*, it is established through the arisen [state] within the framework of the four mudrās. Thus, the *karmamudrā* is to be understood as the state of being an ācārya.
But is it not also stated that there is the consecration of the flask (*kalaśābhiṣeka*) for all six, since the operation of the flask occurs everywhere?
How then is it that the word "kalaśa" (jar) functions here as an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the breast, since this [functioning] also occurs through the operation of the breast?
He demonstrates all of this [as follows]: "When that which is intended by the Teacher and others is purified by means of laughter and so forth..."
This distinction is established by its arising, and not from an inherent nature once produced;
for it is variegated in its manifestation, like a gem that undergoes heating before being polished, resulting in pleasure.
One should understand the reality of the Guru: when one ceases from the act of friction, there is bliss (rama).
Due to its variegated nature and the existence of the grasped and the grasper, it is "variegated" (citra); bliss (ānanda) lasts until the friction, up to the limit of the rubbing.
And because it is said that "the friction of the bodhicitta" is the contact up to the vicinity of the jewel (*maṇi*),

and "the supreme [friction]" is that which occurs before the jewel, it is understood that there is a ripening (*pāka*) from ordinary pleasure into the presence of intense bliss; this supreme ripening extends from the jewel forward to the tip of the jewel (*ratnāgra*).
The phrase "the reality of the guru" has already been explained.

*Virama* (cessation) refers to the cessation [of emission]; when the *bodhicitta* falls, through the process of *vimarda* (churning), one reflects, "Happiness has been enjoyed by me"—this reflection is *virama*. This *virama* is the fourth, which is likewise that very thing: the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*), whose intrinsic nature is the primordial state (*prakṛtisvabhāva*).

Furthermore, when that which consists of the dependent origination of the form of transformation is known in that very same manner as before, it becomes the fourth [joy]; and these four joys in the external consort, the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), are established within the system of the four seals, where one joy— by virtue of being situated therein— is called the "action-seal."
And here, the systematic arrangement of the formless [wisdom] and so forth should be understood as being stated in the context of the "forceful initiation" (haṭhaseka):
having attained the action-seal (karmamudrā), one should meditate upon the dharma-seal (dharmamudrā);
above that is the great seal (mahāmudrā), from which the pledge-seal (samayamudrā) arises.
Because the activity (*karman*) of body, speech, and mind is of an innate nature (*sahajarūpa*), it is a seal (*mudrā*). It is marked (*aṅkita*) as the action-seal (*karmamudrā*);

and because she is the support for that [activity], by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) and for the sake of indication (*upalakṣaṇārtha*), it is the playful woman (*lalana*) herself who is so called.

Furthermore, that wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*) which is described as having the nature of the *sahaja* (innate) upon attaining the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), is in reality merely a form of transformation; because it merely imitates the innate, it is called the "outflow fruit" (*niṣyandaphala*). Thus, within the outflow, there is the "variegated," which is bliss itself. Then, through the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*), phenomena such as blue, yellow, and so forth, having first been purified as deities, are devoid of being objects of perception and the like. Consequently, they become the supreme bliss, the singular beauty, the means, and the very nature of the *dharmadhātu*. That which has reached the state of investigation and is non-abiding in form is the *dharma-mudrā*.

And this [result] is the *vipākaphala* (ripened fruit), because it is distinguished as the path by virtue of being the proximate cause of Mahāmudrā. At that moment of ripening, there is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).

Then, through the sealing with the three mudrās, and by reflecting that "this is both great and a mudrā," one realizes—through diligent and uninterrupted practice of the knowledge of the path whose nature is non-abiding—the Mahāmudrā. It is devoid of intrinsic nature, free from the obscurations of the knowable and so forth, the support of all perfections, having the single nature of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, and having the single form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) whose body is objectless great compassion. This is Mahāmudrā.
And this is the fruit of stainlessness (*vaimalya-phala*) due to the departure of all obscurations;
and in that moment characterized by distinctness, there is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).

Furthermore, the "pledge" (*samaya*) is the convention (*saṅketa*); for the sake of sentient beings, it is the miraculous manifestation (*vikurvaṇa*) of Vajradhara in the form of Heruka and others, whose nature is that of the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) and the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), which is the Pledge Seal (*samayamudrā*).
And this is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*); therein lies the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*),
wherein the [various] seals (*mudrā*) possess the nature of causes in relation to each preceding one.

And because each subsequent one depends upon the previous, the state of being a fruit now belongs to each seal (mudrā) individually. He states that they possess the nature of the four joys: "The joys belong to each seal, yet without the Great Seal (mahāmudrā);
this is known from scripture, from one's own self-awareness, and from the instruction of the Guru."
Each individual mudrā should be understood as having four joys, excluding the Mahāmudrā;
for this very purpose, he states three reasons beginning with "from scripture" (āgamāt) and so forth.

For thus the scripture states in the *Hevajra* and other tantras: "In the *vicitra* [stage] there is the first bliss (*prathamānanda*); in the *vipāka* [stage], the supreme bliss (*paramānanda*); in the *vimarda*, the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*); and in the *vilakṣaṇa* [stage], the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). By such passages, the nature of the *ānandas* and so forth is declared for the *vicitra* and other stages;
therefore, the arrangement of the *ānandas* and so forth occurs precisely where the *vicitra* and others arise.
And its manifestation occurs only in the three mudrās, not in the mahāmudrā;
this meaning is indeed clear as the nature of self-awareness,
and the instruction of the true guru will be explained later in the passage beginning with "vicitra" and so forth.
The physical *karmamudrā* has been described as having the nature of the four joys (*caturānanda*).
Now he speaks of the verbal *dharmamudrā*, which likewise has the nature of the four joys: "From the *karmamudrā* comes the *vicitra* [joy]; the *vipāka* is the state of being the self of the world;
stability is the *vilakṣaṇa*; therein, the *vimarda* is the beholding of the world. (28)

From the *karmamudrā*, by means of the sign (*nimitta*) and through the oral instruction of the true guru, the state of being the self of the world (*jagadātmatā*) is perceived by speech as a manifold manifestation (*citrollekha*); this very state is "diverse" (*vicitra*).
Furthermore, through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) directed toward penetration (*nirvedha*), because the manifold manifestations have subsided, it is the "ripened fruit" (*vipāka*).
Within that state of being the self of the world, the stability of non-manifestation (*anullekha*) resulting from the excellence of cultivation is what is "distinct" (*vilakṣaṇa*).

Thus, although the yogin who possesses the realization of the world’s nature as emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects remains stable, he nevertheless acts in that very same way through his conviction in non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhāna-adhimokṣa*). His observation and contemplation of the world is "the crushing" (*vimarda*). Here too, the fourfold bliss (*ānanda-catuṣṭaya*) is to be applied sequentially to these various stages;
and in this case as well, the fourth is "that again, just so," being the fourth as before.

And when, by the statement "the single bliss of the gods (sura-tānanda) alone is delimited by the number four," all is of the nature of the Innate (sahaja), then the Dharma-mudrā is the Supreme Bliss (paramānanda) alone, which is the single form of the four joys.

Having spoken of the Dharma-mudrā, he now describes the mental Mahāmudrā, whose sole nature is innate bliss (sahajānanda): "Non-abiding in all things is proclaimed as Mahāmudrā; because of the purity of self-awareness, there is no possibility of the manifold [appearances] and so forth. (29)
"In all things" refers to the non-abiding, non-mental engagement, and non-superimposition regarding the dependently originated aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth.
As it is said in the scriptures: "Non-mental engagements are wholesome; mental engagements are unwholesome."
Likewise—O you whose intentions are free from conceptual construction, whose mind is non-abiding, who are without recollection or mental engagement, and who are without support; homage be to you!
Thus, in this context, one should not consider [the practice] to be impossible to perform— like the instruction for the ornament of the crest-jewel of Takṣaka that removes fever—
for by the grace of the feet of a true guru, it is certainly possible to directly perceive Mahāmudrā, which is characterized by the possession of all excellent forms.
Now, one might ask: why is it not of the nature of four moments here?

He replies: because self-awareness is stainless, due to its purity, there is no possibility here of the three stained moments beginning with the "variegated" (vicitra); consequently, the three joys (ānanda) do not occur.

Now, one might raise the doubt that non-abiding is inconceivability, and that when it is being conceived, it is merely a defilement because it acts as an obscuration. To dispel this doubt, he says: "For that knowledge which is effortless is declared to be inconceivable;
indeed, that which is inconceivable [only] after having been deliberately conceived would not truly be inconceivable. (30)
"Effortless," and so forth:
that non-abiding, inconceivable gnosis does not arise from analytical investigation; rather, how could it be effortless and attained through its own inherent nature?
From what [source]?
Having reflected and deliberated, that which is to be thought about does not thereby become unthinkable.

As it is said in the *Jñānasiddhi*: "Buddha-knowledge is therefore remembered as effortless and non-conceptual; yet, because of the absence of a cause for reflection, there is no state of being devoid of thought."
Thus it is said.

Now, in order to refute the apprehension of [the world as mere] consciousness and the apprehension of nihilism that might arise upon its removal, he says: "But those who perceive suchness in accordance with the meaning of the Middle Way—they alone are the knowers of reality and are blessed, provided they have direct perception through their own awareness. (39)
Regarding the passage beginning with "tathatām" (suchness):

those who perceive—that is, directly realize—suchness, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), by following the meaning of the Middle Way and being free from the four extremes, are the fortunate ones who know reality. What need is there for them to rely on nihilism?

If that reality were not experienced through consciousness—that is, through the act of perceiving—because it would then be devoid of all mental constructs (*ullekha*), it could not be directly perceived.

And this [reality], which consists of the two truths, is free from both extremes, inseparable from emptiness and compassion, and has the nature of wisdom and means; it is to be known by one who has gained insight through the grace of the feet of a true guru.
He states that very point with its supplementary explanation: "Whatever superimposition there may be, all of it is in every way non-existent;
for the meaning of the Middle Way is free from superimposition—how then could there be negation or affirmation therein? (32)

Regarding the passage beginning with "as much as" (*yāvān*): because therein, whatever superimposition (*samāropa*) or conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding the meaning of the middle way exists, none of that is present;
such an absence of superimposition is also accepted in the system of Vijñānavāda.
Therefore, he says "in every respect" (*sarvathā*);
for in that case, there exists for consciousness a basis for the superimposition (*samāropa*) of real existence (*vastusattva*),
and thus there is not an absence of superimposition in every respect therein.
By this, the doctrine of the "illusion-like" (māyopama) is also refuted.
Why?

Let alone for now the fact that all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have exclusion (*apoha*) as their object; even in the Vijñānavāda, it is possible for there to be no superimposition (*nirāropa*).
Therefore, the meaning of the Middle Way is free from superimposition and free from conceptual proliferation;
this is the supreme distinction.

Even in the Vijñānavāda, although there is non-conceptuality, due to the power of ignorance—the existence of which is extremely firm—even if there is no direct mental delineation at that very moment, the apprehension of the feeling is indeed clear upon the fact of self-awareness.
Is it not the case that this is equally true for you as well, since all conceptual constructions are absent in the state of the "back" (the ultimate)?

Because there is no fixed abode and because one conforms to sentient beings who have no such abode, [all is] conventional usage; therefore, in that case, how could there be affirmation or negation—that is, the establishment or the exclusion [of anything]?
The meaning is that they do not exist at all.
If that is so, how are the entities being perceived known?
To this he says: "In the absence of the superimposition of knowledge and the object of knowledge, there is no conceiving therein; otherwise it is not so.
Everything is as it was before; for it is not as the intellect [conceives it]. (33)
Regarding the passage beginning with "In knowledge," etc.:

for in that reality-natured world, which is empty of the superimposition of knowledge and the knowable, conceptualization (*manyanā*)—whether discursive (*savikalpa*) or non-discursive (*nirvikalpa*)—is not otherwise.
How then [does it occur]?

Just as it was previously stated regarding the ignorance of reality, so too it has been said regarding the knowledge of reality: "Nothing is to be removed from this, nor is anything at all to be added;
one who sees the real as it truly is, being a seer of reality, is liberated."
Thus it is stated elsewhere as well: "The full comprehension of existence itself is called nirvāṇa."

Alternatively, "all is just as it was before" means that just as the world is of the nature of the innate (*sahaja*) and the nature of suchness (*tathatā*) when there is no awakening, so too should it be understood upon awakening; as it has been said: "As it was before, so it is after; you have realized suchness."
Thus, it is said elsewhere: "For all phenomena have an innate nature (*sahaja-gatika*); they do not transcend that nature."
Likewise, even in the absence of Buddhas, the *dharmatā* remains exactly as it is;
such is the detailed explanation,
and this is the supreme distinction.
Just as previously the intellect was determined by the subject-object dichotomy and so forth, in that very same way there is nothing else;
as it has been said: "These phenomena, however, are Nirvana itself, appearing in the form of saṃsāra due to delusion."

And here, delusion (*moha*) is the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the grasped, the grasper, and so forth; likewise it has been stated elsewhere: "O Saraha, speak thus: that which is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), however it may be understood, does not become that [which it is conceptually determined to be]."
Thus [it is said].

Having thus understood such knowledge, he shows the world as it truly is; for by means of that [knowledge], the world is realized as unborn. Through awakening, his own intellect is purified, and for that wise one, the world is real through effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "By whom," etc., and ending with "because of the impossibility of the arising of the existent and non-existent": the world, which is unborn, has been perceived—that is, known through direct perception—by him; his intellect, being dependently originated, is indeed pure by virtue of its awakening (*bodha*) and penetration (*nirvedha*).
Therefore, for that wise one, the world is his own innate reality (*satya*), which is non-false, even without effort—that is, without exertion.

Now he shows that even conceptual construction is nirvāṇa: "This conceptual construction, which arises dependently and whose connection [to reality] has not been discerned—that very thing is nirvāṇa; do not, O mind, fall into delusion. (35)
"Unmanifested," and so forth:
this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), whose connection [to its object] is unmanifested—that is, whose connection is unknown—is dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
Therefore, this very [construction] is itself *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, O mind, do not be deluded;
for it has been said: "That which is dependent origination, that itself is considered by you to be emptiness."
And emptiness is nirvana.
It shows how Mahāmudrā is attained through the awakening to unborn knowledge:
"He who stands in the antidote, who is neither attached to reality nor [to its opposite], and who has no craving for the fruit—he finds Mahāmudrā. (36)
"Antidote," and so forth.

"Antidote" refers to that which does not abide at all because of the avoidance—through non-mental engagement—of attachment to the conceptualization that defines the antidotes consisting of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom by way of defining their intrinsic nature, qualities, and essence.

By means of abandoning attachment to the conceptualization that defines the antidotes, one should also understand the abandonment of attachment to the conceptualization that defines the discordant factors (vipakṣa), which consist of the five appropriated aggregates such as form and so forth, along with their outflows.
Because the absence of that [the latter] necessarily entails the absence of this [the former].

"Even one who is attached to reality" means one who is not at all attached—that is, not even clinging—to the conceptualization that investigates reality as having the nature of emptiness, suchness, and so forth, by way of defining its intrinsic nature and other characteristics.

"One for whom there is no greed for the fruit" means one who has no greed—that is, no longing—for the fruit, which consists of the conceptual attachment to the investigation of attaining everything from the first stage up to the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
He finds and attains Mahāmudrā.

By this, he describes Mahāmudrā as being liberated from all attachment, through the absence of attachment to the adverse factors, their remedies, reality, and the fruit—because the world has the nature of being non-abiding and free from superimposition.
In that case, is there a total absence of the perfection of generosity and the other perfections within Mahāmudrā?
No;
for that very [perfection] consists of the two accumulations of merit and wisdom, which have all the perfections as their essence.
As it is said in the *Viśeṣacintibrahmaparipṛcchā-mahāyāna-sūtra*: "That which is the complete relinquishing of all afflictions—this is generosity."
That which is non-conditioning is this morality; that which is signlessness is this patience; that which is seclusion is this vigor.
"That which is non-abiding is this meditation; that which is the absence of conceptual proliferation is this wisdom.
By this it is established that the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) consists precisely in the nature of non-abiding and the absence of conceptual proliferation.
As it is said in the *Saptashatikā*, the Blessed One said:
"Mañjuśrī, at the time when you cultivate the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), upon what do you rely while cultivating the perfection of wisdom?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Blessed One, at whatever time I cultivate the perfection of wisdom,
at that time I cultivate the perfection of wisdom without being established anywhere.
The Blessed One said:
"Mañjuśrī, for you who are non-abiding, what is the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom?
Mañjuśrī replied,
"Lord, that very cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is that which is non-abiding anywhere."
The Blessed One said:
"Mañjuśrī, at the time when you cultivate the perfection of wisdom, which of your roots of merit at that time undergoes increase or decrease?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Blessed One, at that time, not even the slightest root of virtue of mine undergoes increase or decrease.
Blessed One, that which involves the increase or decrease of any dharma whatsoever does not cultivate the perfection of wisdom.
Blessed One, that cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is not to be recognized as such which stands for the sake of the increase or decrease of any dharma whatsoever."
“O Blessed One, that cultivation of the perfection of wisdom is such that it neither abandons the dharmas of ordinary beings nor appropriates the dharmas of a Buddha,” and so forth.

Having spoken of Mahāmudrā, whose nature consists of the four joys and who is omnipresent, he speaks of Samayamudrā: "Just as the arrangement of joy and the other [blisses] occurs in the case of Karmamudrā, so too does it occur in the case of Samayamudrā through the grace of the Vajrācārya. (37)
"Yathaiva" and so forth.
"By the grace of the Vajrācārya" means by the instruction of the true guru.
In this regard, the instruction is as follows:

From the *mahāmudrā*, when the Blessed One arises in the form of enjoyment (*saṃbhogarūpa*) together with wisdom (*prajñā*)—which is the nature of the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*)—there is *ānanda* from the point of friction up to the jewel (*maṇi*). Beyond the jewel is *paramānanda*. When there occurs a state of melting due to great passion (*mahārāga*), the two drops (*bindu*) situated in the middle of the union of the moon and sun—the forms of wisdom and method—take the form of two drops by being joined together above and below; this is *sahajānanda*.
Thus it has been said: "Therein is neither end nor middle; there is neither worldly existence nor liberation. This indeed is that supreme great bliss—neither other, nor the self."
Furthermore, this has a twofold meaning according to its interpretable and definitive nature. Among these,
the definitive meaning is non-conceptual cognition regarding that very kind of extraordinary reality.
And it is of interpretable meaning.
It is not that the first dot is not [there], nor is it that the last is not [there].
"Because it is continuous there, in the absence of a center, there is no 'middle' there;
therefore, it is not of the nature of existence (*bhava*).
The *bindu* at the junction of the sun of means (*upāya*) is existence."
He is not reality;
he is neither *nirvāṇa* nor of the nature of *nirvāṇa*. United with the moon of wisdom, he whose essential nature is the union of both hands is this very supreme great bliss (*paramamahāsukha*).
In this state, there is no cognition of another or of a self.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the designations such as Vajrasattva and so forth, which were previously mentioned, are established here as being like the innate (*sahaja*) state through the *karmamudrā*.

Then, following the exhortation by the songs of the four goddesses, Pukkasī and the others, when the Blessed One arises in the form of the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogarūpa*) like one awakened from sleep, the observation made by way of pure mundane conceptualization for the sake of sentient beings is the *virama*.
Here too, it is the fourth because of the phrase "that again, likewise";
"that" refers to what is perceived as the innate (*sahaja*),
and "again" means in all its aspects.
The word "thus" (tathā) should be understood as being like the Innate (sahaja), because of the statement: "The single bliss of sexual union (suratānanda) is divided into four categories.
When everything is of the nature of the Innate, then the Samaya-mudrā consists of the four joys;
[in that state] there is only the Joy of Cessation (viramānanda).
But surely, here the formless experience is clearly shown by way of its nature as the *bindu*.
No;
for even then, because it consists of inexpressible bliss, there is no obstruction to the manifestation of the forms of the entire universe within that which is formless.

If that is so, for what purpose is the arising in the form of the *bindu*? For here too, it is logical that it consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) in the form of arms, face, and so forth, just like the bliss obtained through the *karmamudrā*.
It is said in reply:

it is for the sake of manifesting with form (*sākāra-khyāti*) through the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), by way of the nature of the *bindu*, just as the form of a jar arises from the form of clay.
As it has been said: "It abides in the form of a drop (*bindu*).
Now, it should be stated thus: "The closed [state] resembles a jasmine flower (*kunda*), while the open [state] has the nature of bliss.
That which is attained through the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) is the closed state, which is not the ultimate reality (*aparamārtha*).
Nirvāṇa is disclosed and unobstructed;
thus, happiness is indeed distinct [from suffering].
That too is not so.
"He would not exist having abandoned bliss," because there is no bliss distinct [from it] due to the identity (*tādātmya*) of the drop (*bindu*) and bliss;
and this is to be understood from the statement: "Therefore, that which is called 'bliss' is not a great element (*mahābhūta*), since bliss is [the reality] known as the *tattva*."
Now, if this is the thought:
"By assuming the form of the various *bindus*, it is indeed formless"—
that too is not tenable.

If this is stated with the intention that [the supreme] is formless (*nirākāra*), then, setting aside the *bindu* which is the cause for doubting whether consciousness is formless, only pleasure (*sāta*) alone would have been described as supreme.
What is the use of this *bindu*, burdened as it is by the aforementioned effort?
Therefore, the formless does not exist at all.

This very point just mentioned clarifies that each mudrā possesses its own distinct bliss: the *karmamudrā* is the *vicitra* (diversity) [bliss], the *dharmamudrā* is born of ripening (*vipākaja*), the *mahāmudrā* is the *vilakṣaṇa* (distinctive), and the *samayamudrā* is the *vimarda* (dissolution).
"Variegated," and so forth; the meaning has already been explained.
If it is argued that this text follows the lineage of the four mudrās,
and that it conforms to the Yoginītantras rather than the Yogatantras,
that is not so.
It is said by the noble Nāgārjuna, in accordance with the *Śrī-samāja*:
that which is [taught] through five stages is now explained in terms of the four seals (*caturmudrā*).

The two sequences consist respectively in the realization of the mantra-body and of consciousness; and these two are here taught by means of a single mudrā, for the purpose of establishing the mind in the state of the mantra-body.
Since the bliss of the Dharma-seal is the vision of the relative truth, and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is the truth itself, it is called the meaning of the Great Seal (mahāmudrā).
The fruit of the pledge-seal (samayamudrā) is the experience of non-duality within duality; it is the divine union of the stages that bestows the fruit of Buddhahood.

And likewise, it was stated by the venerable master Candrakīrti in his commentary *Pradīpoddyotana* on the six parameters (*ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā*): "The stage of generation (*utpattikrama*) should come first, which accomplishes the form of the mantra; the second stage is said to be the mere contemplation of the mind (*cittanidhyaptimātra*)."
The third stage, however, is the delightful vision of the truth within the conventional; the fourth stage is said to be the purification of the conventional through the truth.
The fifth is called "the union" (yuganaddha), which is the conjunction of the two truths; this is the supreme limb of practice, a compendium of the meaning of all tantras.
He who knows the many variations of these sequences through the method of expansion (prastāra), as well as their synthesis, is indeed a knower of the Tantra.

Likewise, the venerable Āryadeva also provided a summary of the five stages (*pañcakrama*) in the *Sūtaka-melāpaka* by means of the names: the reality of mantra (*mantratattva*), the reality of the seal (*mudrātattva*), the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*), the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*), and the reality of the deity (*devatātattva*).

In that context, "the reality of mantra" refers to the form of Hevajra and others arising from the *hūṃ* syllable and other such mantras. "The reality of the seal" refers, according to the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) through the sequence of numerical calculation, to the mere contemplation of the mind; however, according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), it refers to the action seal (*karmamudrā*). "The reality of the self" refers to the fact that the world is a manifold of consciousness devoid of intrinsic nature.
The reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*) is the non-arising of phenomena.

The reality of the deity (*devatātattva*) is the identification of the reality of the self and the reality of phenomena—that is to say, their non-differentiation. These five realities, according to the instruction of the gurus, should be applied to the four *mudrās* in sequence, just as in the Five Stages (*pañcakrama*).
